dialectic-of-sex: In The Dialectic of Sex (1970), Shulamith Firestone reworked Marx and Engels to argue that the deepest form of oppression is not class but sex, rooted in the biological facts of reproduction and the family structures built around them. She contended that women's subordination originates in the reproductive division of labor and that genuine liberation would require freeing women from biology itself, including through reproductive technology. The book was a founding text of radical feminism, pressing the claim that overturning patriarchy demands transforming, not merely reforming, the family and the sexual order.
gender-performativity: Gender performativity is Judith Butler's thesis that gender is not the expression of a stable inner essence but is constituted through repeated acts, gestures, and stylizations of the body that produce the illusion of a natural, fixed identity. On this view there is no 'doer behind the deed': the appearance of an underlying gendered self is an effect of the very performances it seems to cause. Developed in Gender Trouble (1990), the idea challenges the assumption that sex grounds gender and opens space for understanding how norms can be subverted through their own repetition.
heteronormativity: Heteronormativity names the web of social norms, institutions, and assumptions that treat heterosexuality as the default, natural, and privileged form of sexuality and organize gender and family life accordingly. It describes how a culture can make opposite-sex desire and the traditional gender binary seem self-evident, marginalizing other orientations and identities as deviations. Associated with Judith Butler and queer theory more broadly, the concept exposes how such norms are produced and enforced rather than simply given by nature.
mackinnon-dominance: Catharine MacKinnon's dominance approach reframes sex inequality not as a matter of irrational difference between the sexes but as a system in which men hold power and women are subordinated. On this account sexuality itself is socially constructed around male dominance, so practices like pornography and sexual harassment are not marginal excesses but mechanisms that eroticize and entrench that hierarchy. MacKinnon argued that law should confront this inequality directly, treating pornography as a civil-rights harm rather than protected expression.
birdcage-oppression: Marilyn Frye's birdcage image illustrates why oppression is often invisible when examined one piece at a time. Looking at a single wire of a birdcage, one cannot see why it would confine a bird, which could simply fly around it; only by stepping back to see the whole network of wires does the trap become clear. Frye used this to argue that oppression consists of a systematic, interlocking set of barriers and forces that mutually reinforce one another, so that each restriction on women appears trivial in isolation while together they constrain a whole group.
five-faces-oppression: Iris Marion Young argued that oppression is not a single phenomenon but a family of distinct conditions, and she identified five 'faces': exploitation, marginalization, powerlessness, cultural imperialism, and violence. Rather than locating injustice solely in the deliberate acts of a tyrant, she showed how structural relations and everyday practices can systematically disadvantage social groups. The framework lets one recognize that different groups may be oppressed in different ways, and that a group can suffer some faces of oppression without suffering all of them.
intersectionality: Intersectionality, a term introduced by legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw, holds that systems of power such as racism and sexism do not operate independently but intersect to produce distinctive forms of disadvantage. Crenshaw showed that Black women, for instance, can face harms that neither antiracist nor feminist frameworks alone capture, because their experience falls at the crossing of multiple axes of identity. The concept has become a central analytic tool for understanding how race, gender, class, sexuality, and other categories combine to shape people's social positions.
double-consciousness: Double consciousness is W.E.B. Du Bois's description, in The Souls of Black Folk (1903), of the divided self-awareness produced by living within a society that devalues one's race. He wrote of the sense of 'always looking at one's self through the eyes of others' and of feeling one's 'twoness'—being both American and Black in a nation that grants full recognition to neither together. The concept captures the psychological strain of measuring oneself by the standards of a world that regards one with contempt or pity.
racial-contract: In The Racial Contract (1997), Charles W. Mills argued that the familiar social-contract tradition of Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau conceals an unspoken agreement among those classified as white to establish and maintain a global order of racial domination. On this reading, the abstract 'persons' of contract theory were tacitly restricted to white men, while nonwhite peoples were excluded from full personhood and subjected to conquest and exploitation. Mills used the idea to expose how a supposedly neutral political philosophy has underwritten and normalized white supremacy.
black-skin-white-masks: Black Skin, White Masks (1952) is Frantz Fanon's psychological and philosophical study of how colonialism and racism deform the inner life of the colonized. Drawing on psychoanalysis, phenomenology, and his own experience, Fanon analyzed how a racist world can lead Black people to internalize inferiority and to strive to assume the values, language, and self-image of the white colonizer. The work is a foundational text of anticolonial thought, examining the alienation imposed by a society that fixes people within a devalued racial identity.
cosmopolitanism-ethics: Cosmopolitanism, as developed by Kwame Anthony Appiah, is the ethical stance that all human beings belong to a single moral community and owe one another obligations that cross the borders of nation, culture, and creed. Appiah pairs this universal concern with a respect for particular, legitimate differences, arguing that we can take an interest in others' distinct ways of life without abandoning the conviction that some values are shared. His version emphasizes conversation across difference as the practical means by which strangers can come to understand and live with one another.
epistemic-injustice: Epistemic injustice, a concept named by Miranda Fricker, is a wrong done to someone specifically in their capacity as a knower. She distinguished two main forms: testimonial injustice, in which prejudice leads a hearer to give a speaker's word less credibility than it deserves, and hermeneutical injustice, in which gaps in a society's shared interpretive resources leave some group unable to make sense of their own experiences. The idea shows that unfairness can operate not only in the distribution of goods but in whose knowledge and understanding are recognized.
objectification: Objectification is the treatment of a person as a mere object or instrument rather than as a being with dignity, autonomy, and a subjectivity of their own. In feminist philosophy it names especially the reduction of a person, most often a woman, to a body or a set of parts valued for the use or pleasure of others, denying full agency and moral standing. Philosophers such as Martha Nussbaum have analyzed it into distinct elements—like instrumentality, denial of autonomy, and fungibility—to clarify when and why treating someone as an object is wrong.
disability-philosophy: The philosophy of disability examines what disability is, how it should be understood, and what justice requires in relation to it. A central debate contrasts the 'medical model,' which locates disability in an individual's bodily impairment, with the 'social model,' which locates it in the way societies are built and organized to exclude people whose bodies or minds differ from an assumed norm. The field also addresses questions of well-being, autonomy, accommodation, and the value of disabled lives, challenging assumptions that treat disability as simply a deficit.
male-gaze: The male gaze names the way visual culture, and film in particular, tends to present the world from a heterosexual masculine point of view, positioning women as objects to be looked at rather than as active subjects. The concept was crystallized by film theorist Laura Mulvey, who drew on psychoanalysis to argue that classical cinema structures pleasure around a male spectator and a passive, eroticized female image. It has become a widely used tool for analyzing how images shape and encode relations of power between the sexes.
